headline: High: Claude Code’s writable, networked terminal agent can conflict with a local game-simulation repo, but direct injection and leakage paths are limited by B’s no-network profile.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can read repo files and user-provided directories, and B is a codebase/simulation artifact with no documented output channel into A. The only plausible bridge is manual copy-paste or files in the shared cwd, so injection is possible but not default and the blast radius is limited.
conditions: IF the operator copies B-generated text into A’s terminal session, prompt injection becomes possible.
IF both agents are pointed at the same writable workspace, A may ingest attacker-controlled file content from B’s outputs.
mitigations: Keep B outputs out of shared files; use separate directories.
Review any copied text before pasting into A.
Disable automatic ingestion of generated artifacts into A.
Use read-only mounts for B outputs where possible.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for files passed between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches source code, git history, shell environment, and files in cwd, while B has no network egress and no declared data classes. There is no documented direct data path from B to a third party, so leakage risk is mainly local workspace exposure rather than exfiltration.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in the shared cwd, A can read them while operating.
IF B is extended to emit artifacts into the same workspace, those artifacts may be visible to A.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace.
Use separate per-agent directories.
Rotate or remove credentials from the cwd before running A.
Set restrictive file permissions on sensitive files.
requires-engineering: isolate agents with separate mounts or containers.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and broad network egress; B is a runnable simulation/repo artifact with no concurrency controls documented. Shared filesystem/git state is the only stated overlap, so concurrent writes can conflict even though B itself has no write capability documented.
conditions: IF B is run against the same git checkout that A edits, file and git-state conflicts can occur.
IF the operator lets both agents write to the same directory, last-writer-wins corruption is possible.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own clone or worktree.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Commit or stash A’s changes before B runs.
Use file locks for shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking around shared git state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate code or shell actions from repo context, and B is a game-playing/simulation project with no verification or critique role documented. If B consumes A’s outputs as authoritative artifacts, errors can cascade into incorrect repo changes or simulation behavior, though B’s no-network profile limits downstream harm.
conditions: IF B treats A-produced files or instructions as ground truth, A’s mistakes propagate.
IF A’s generated code is committed without review, downstream simulation behavior may be wrong.
mitigations: Require human review of A outputs before B uses them.
Add a validation step between A and B.
Compare A-generated artifacts against tests or linting.
Reject unverified instructions from shared files.
requires-engineering: implement schema checks for inter-agent handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles git credentials and shell environment data, while B declares no data classes and no residency or retention constraints. The pair does not show a direct compliance mismatch, but A’s secret handling means any shared workspace could create a minor policy exposure; B is not cited for a specific compliance regime because none is documented.
conditions: IF secrets are stored in files under the shared workspace, A may expose them during normal operation.
IF the operator subjects B to regulated data without a documented policy, compliance review is required.
mitigations: Remove secrets from shared directories.
Use separate retention policies for each workspace.
Document which data classes may enter A’s terminal session.
Audit git history for accidental secret commits.
requires-engineering: formalize residency and retention controls for both agents.
